title: IQueryable and expression trees
body: LINQ has two worlds. `IEnumerable<T>` operators take delegates and run your lambdas in memory. `IQueryable<T>` operators take `Expression<Func<...>>`: the compiler turns the lambda into a data structure describing the code, so a provider such as Entity Framework Core can translate it to SQL or another query language.

The same lambda text can become either a delegate or an expression tree depending on the target type. `Func<int, bool> f = x => x > 2;` compiles to code; `Expression<Func<int, bool>> e = x => x > 2;` compiles to a tree with a `Parameter`, a `Constant` and a `GreaterThan` node that you can inspect, rewrite or compile with `e.Compile()`.

Providers can only translate what they understand. Calling your own C# method inside a query is fine in memory but a database provider throws at runtime because it cannot turn the method into SQL. Expression lambdas also cannot contain statement bodies, assignments or some newer syntax.

Switching from `IQueryable` to `IEnumerable` with `AsEnumerable()` moves the rest of the query into memory: filtering after that point downloads every row first. Keep filters and projections on the queryable side when a database is involved.
Check the static type of a query variable: `IQueryable<T>` means the predicate becomes data for a provider, `IEnumerable<T>` means it runs as your code, possibly after fetching everything.

challenge: Build an expression Expression<Func<string, bool>> that tests s.Length > 3 using the Expression factory methods (Parameter, Property, Constant, GreaterThan, Lambda), print it, and use the compiled delegate to filter ["to", "tree", "leaf"].
question: What does assigning a lambda to `Expression<Func<int, bool>>` produce?
correct: A tree of objects describing the lambda's code
wrong: A compiled delegate identical to Func<int, bool>
reasoning: Expression trees are data a provider can inspect and translate; Compile() turns them into a delegate.
